osmTags.name: Knaresborough Castle
osmTags.description: Norman castle, largely dismantled by the Parliamentarians during Civil War

osmTags.inscription: On 3rd October 1865 the townsfolk forcibly asserted their longstanding public right of access over Castle Yard, which had been denied them by Dr. John Simpson of Castle Lodge.
Originally the Tollbooth, rebuilt in 1768, the building served as The Sessions House dealing with infringements of the law.
The mouldings and roof structure of these buildings indicate a probable date before 1500 ... it was listed in the Survey of 1611 as a hospital for six poor folk.
A pharmacy from at least 1720, when John Beckwith was the apothecary... The shop ceased to be a pharmacy in 1997.
In the 13th Century a Jewish community lived and worshipped in Knaresborough. The Synagogue was situated at the exit to Synagogue Lane
In 1310 Edward II confirmed Wednesday as Market day in Knaresborough by Royal Charter.
In Tudor times the manufacture of linen began as a cottage industry in Knaresborough which later become renowned for 'the finest cloth'.  This former flax mill dating from 1808 ...

Eugene Aram was an 18th century schoolteacher who lived and taught here in White Horse Yard ... notorious for his supposed involvement in the murder of another resident, Daniel Clarke ... Aram was executed at York on 6th August 1759.
This wood frame, grade 2-listed building was built c1208 around a still existing oak tree, as a hunting lodge for King John... A 400 year old mulberry tree planted by James 1st is still fruiting...
This building is on the site of a manorial corn mill dating from Norman times.  The will of the miller in 1656 showed he was making indigo dye from woad probably grown locally.
The frontage of the building to your right is all that remains of one of Knaresborough's oldest industrial buildings. Erected in 1610...
Built in 1764 Castle Mills is a Grade 2 listed building. From 1770 to 1972 it was a flax mill producing fine quality linen.

World War I Centenary Commemoration 11th November 2018. They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old: Age shall not weary them, nor the years condemn. At the going down of the sun and in the morning. We will remember them.

All that remains of the original Market Cross is the circular base which dates from 1709. In 1824 the engineer John Malam, who had contracted to supply gas to the town, took down the stone cross and replaced it, at his own expense with a gas lamp...

First documented in 1206 in the reign of King John the right to hold a market was officially confirmed by a charter of King Edward II to his favourite, Piers Gaveston, then Lord of Knaresborough, in 1310.

Blind Jack of Knaresborough was born John Metcalf in 1717. Although blinded by small pox at the age of six, he led an exceptionally active life as a musician, guide, horseman, gambler, trader and pioneer civil engineer ...
This Clock was presented to the town by the Rotary Club of Knaresborough to celebrate the Millennium

1892-1979 On this site was born Lord Inman of Knaresborough. A man who, from humble beginnings rose to be Chirman of Charing Cross Hospital, Chairman of the BBC and Lord Privy Seal, whilst maintaining a life long affection for the town of his birth.

eras.label: Mapped site · auto T1
eras.summary: Mapped outline, terrain and present-day surroundings from open data. No historic reconstruction.
eras.basis: Everything drawn is traced from OpenStreetMap ways (ODbL) and the Terrarium elevation tiles. Each element names its OSM way.
eras.conjecture: Walls and buildings without a sourced height are drawn as kerb-high plan lines, never as masses. Closed walls have no gates: none are mapped. The DEM is ~30 m source resolution: it cannot show terraces, ditches or scarps. Nothing historic is depicted.
